paragraphs.source_en: The homogeneity of the Round Head paintings indicates the circulation of ideas and, very probably, of people. On the Tassili Plateau the Round Head sites are accumulated in its central-southern part and are within a few hours or days walk from each other. No wonder the painted motifs are very similar here but this similarity can be also observed in more distant localities, in the Acacus and in the Algerian Tadrart, suggesting a mobility of groups or ideas.

paragraphs.source_en: The mobility of Central Saharan groups in prehistoric times is also testified by the archaeological record. There is an apparent contradiction in the Early Holocene Epipalaeolithic record, namely the increased sedentism versus the high mobility of hunter-gatherers. The stone structures unearthed in some shelters in the Acacus and the Tassili were interpreted as the bases of wind breaks or of more stable huts, and they indicate at least partial sedentism as early as in the 10th millennium BP (Barich 1987). Associated with the structures were grinding stones and pottery, equipment that is difficult to carry on long distances or frequent displacements. Some shelters were therefore used as living places since the earliest phases of the occupation in the Epipalaeolithic period.

paragraphs.source_en: However, these increasingly sedentary hunter-gatherers possessed a lithic industry made from raw material which is only found far from the Acacus and the Tassili. Flint of good quality is always present in the Early Holocene settlements of the Acacus but outcrops of flint are located hundreds of kilometres away (Di Lernia 1999). According to Di Lernia (1999) the procurement, exploitation and circulation of raw materials are very distinctive features of the Epipalaeolithic phase. They exploited not only the local raw materials but also various significant "exotic" stones, such as quartzite and quartz, which are abundant in the neighbouring Messak Settafet.

paragraphs.source_en: The provenance of raw material from the Messak is particularly important as this is the main area of concentration of the Bubaline engravings which may be at least partly contemporaneous with the Round Heads. As mentioned earlier, the Round Head paintings and the Bubaline engravings are not mixed together and they are so different in technique and themes that it is difficult to imagine that they were produced by groups of the same culture and ideology. Supposing that the Epipalaeolithic groups of the Acacus and the Tassili were the producers of the Round Head paintings, the fact that they owned tools that originated from the "other rock-art" territory is significant.
